title: Partition Tree: Conditional Density Estimation over General Outcome Spaces
claim: A tree of sequential splits induces a rectangular partition of the joint space, so each query slice yields a histogram.
layout: 2 panels, tree left and partition right, dotted arrows linking leaves to cells
description: The left panel is a binary decision tree drawn with rounded boxes and black arrows. The root A0 = X×Y splits on y ≤ s1. Its two children, A1 and A2, split on x ≤ t1 and x ≤ t2. The four leaves are A11, A12, A21 and A22, and the edges are labeled with the split conditions. The right panel, titled 'Partition of A0', is a large rectangle with x on the horizontal axis and y on the vertical axis. A horizontal line at s1 divides it into top and bottom halves. A vertical line at t2 splits the top half, and a vertical line at t1 splits the bottom half. This gives four rectangular cells labeled A11, A12, A21 and A22. Dotted curved arrows connect each leaf in the tree to its matching cell. The drawing is black and white, with no color. The eye goes first to the tree root and then follows the dotted links to the partition.
caption: Illustration of a partition of the joint space Z = X × Y. Each leaf of the tree corresponds to a rectangular cell in the induced partition (right). For a fixed query x = t, the leaves whose X-projection contains t form a histogram over Y: the associated Y -intervals AY are the bins, and the estimator is constant on each bin. In particular, for x ≤t1 the slice x = t intersects two leaves, yielding a two-bin histogram defined by A11 and A12; for t1 < x ≤t2, it intersects the leaves A21 and A12. On each cell, the conditional density is estimated from empirical counts normalized by the Y-volume µY (AY ).
abstract: We propose Partition Tree, a tree-based framework for conditional density estimation over general outcome spaces that supports both continuous and categorical variables within a unified formulation. Our approach models conditional distributions as piecewise-constant densities on data-adaptive partitions and learns trees by greedily minimizing a surrogate for conditional log-loss. This yields a scalable alternative to existing probabilistic trees that does not make parametric assumptions about the target distribution. We further introduce Partition Forest, an ensemble extension obtained by averaging conditional densities. Empirically, we demonstrate improved probabilistic prediction over CART-style trees and competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art probabilistic tree methods and Random Forests.
